    private static final long MOD = 998244353L;
    private static final int MAX_SIZE = 400010;
    private static long[] factorial;
    private static long[] inverseFactorial;

    private static void buildTables() {
        factorial = new long[MAX_SIZE];
        inverseFactorial = new long[MAX_SIZE];
        factorial[0] = 1;
        for (int i = 1; i < MAX_SIZE; i++) {
            factorial[i] = (factorial[i - 1] * i) % MOD;
        }
        inverseFactorial[MAX_SIZE - 1] = modPow(factorial[MAX_SIZE - 1], MOD - 2);
        for (int i = MAX_SIZE - 2; i >= 0; i--) {
            inverseFactorial[i] = (inverseFactorial[i + 1] * (i + 1)) % MOD;
        }
    }

    private static long combination(int n, int r) {
        if (r < 0 || r > n) return 0;
        return (factorial[n] * inverseFactorial[r] % MOD) * inverseFactorial[n - r] % MOD;
    }

    private static long modPow(long base, long exponent) {
        long result = 1;
        base %= MOD;
        while (exponent > 0) {
            if ((exponent & 1) == 1) {
                result = (result * base) % MOD;
            }
            base = (base * base) % MOD;
            exponent >>= 1;
        }
        return result;
    }

        int k = input.nextInt();

            return;

        // Actually, for each empty cell to be under attack, every row and column must have at least one rook
        // With n rooks on n x n board, this means exactly one rook per row and per column (a permutation matrix)
        
        // In a permutation matrix, two rooks attack each other if they are in the same row or column with no rook between them
        // But since there's exactly one rook per row and column, rooks only attack each other if they are adjacent in some sense...
        
        // Actually, the problem states: "Two rooks attack each other if they share the same row or column, and there are no other rooks between them"

        // With n rooks on n x n board, to have every row and column contain at least one rook, we need exactly one rook per row and column.

        // Similarly, one rook per column satisfies the condition.
        // But placements with one rook per row AND one rook per column are counted in both.

        // With one rook per row, rooks in the same column attack each other.

        // Wait, no: if there are c_j rooks in a column, they are in different rows. The number of adjacent pairs is c_j - 1 if they're in consecutive rows,

        // But S(n, m) * m! is the number of surjective functions from n elements to m elements, which is also the number of ways to partition n items into m non-empty ordered groups.
        // This is known as the Stirling numbers of the second kind multiplied by m!.
        
        // Alternatively, using inclusion-exclusion: number of ways to have n rooks in n rows and exactly m columns = C(n, m) * sum_{i=0}^{m} (-1)^i * C(m, i) * (m-i)^n.
        // So for m = n - k, it's C(n, n-k) * sum_{i=0}^{n-k} (-1)^i * C(n-k, i) * (n-k-i)^n.
        
        // Then total ways for r = n and c = n-k is C(n, k) * sum_{i=0}^{n-k} (-1)^i * C(n-k, i) * (n-k-i)^n.
        // Similarly for c = n and r = n-k, same number.
        // But when k=0, both cases give the same placements (permutations), so we'd double count.
        // For k=0, the answer should be n! (permutations), and indeed our formula for one case gives C(n,0) * sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^i * C(n,i) * (n-i)^n = n! by inclusion-exclusion (number of surjections from n to n is n!).

        if (k >= n) {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
